hops.title: One-eyed lambs, a mountain lily and a skin-cancer pill
hops.text: In the 1950s, sheep ranchers in Idaho's mountain meadows saw lambs born with a single central eye. The cause was wild corn lily, Veratrum californicum, and the timing was startlingly narrow: in later dosing experiments, exposure on day 13 or 14 of pregnancy gave lambs a range of head and face defects, including cyclopia, while lambs in the day 15 group appeared normal. The plant's main teratogenic alkaloid, cyclopamine, binds Smoothened directly and inhibits canonical Hedgehog signaling. In basal cell carcinoma, the most common human cancer, loss of Patched1 function often leaves Smoothened active. Cyclopamine inspired the search that led to vismodegib, a Smoothened blocker approved in 2012.

sources.citation: Welch et al., Journal of Applied Toxicology 29(5):414-421 (2009)
Macha, Batra & Ganti, Cancer Management and Research 5:197-203 (2013)
Axelson et al., Clinical Cancer Research 19(9):2289-2293 (2013)

image.caption: Cyclopamine from wild corn lily binds Smoothened, inhibits Hedgehog signaling, and inspired a skin-cancer pill.

hops.afterHeading: Reading the slope: a code written in two classes
hops.title: Blind cavefish and their sighted relatives are one species
hops.text: Astyanax mexicanus comes in two forms: silvery, sighted fish in Mexican rivers and pale, blind fish in caves. They are the same species. In cavefish embryos, Hedgehog genes are expressed across a wider zone along the front of the midline, and the domains of Pax6, the Class I factor Shh switches off in the spinal cord, are smaller, with a gap between them. That expanded Hedgehog signaling helps trigger lens cell death, and the small eyes stop growing. Boosting Shh in river-fish embryos during the early window when eyes are sensitive causes abnormal eye development and raises lip taste-bud number; separate experiments link Shh to wider jaws.

sources.citation: Strickler, Yamamoto & Jeffery, Development Genes and Evolution 211(3):138-144 (2001)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pale eyeless cavefish and a silvery sighted river fish swimming together near a cave opening.
image.caption: Expanded Hedgehog signaling helps trigger lens cell death and stalls eye growth in cavefish embryos.

hops.afterHeading: The top of the tube: BMPs from the epidermis and roof plate
hops.title: Bone morphogenetic protein in an animal with no bones
hops.text: The name suggests the spinal cord borrowed a skeleton-building factor. It is an accident of history. In 1965 Marshall Urist reported that decalcified bone implanted in muscle induced new bone, and in 1971 he and his colleague Strates called the active factor bone morphogenetic protein. Fruit flies have no bones, yet they use a close relative of BMP4 to pattern their dorsal-ventral axis. In 1993 a team replaced the signaling region in a fly gene fragment with human BMP4's, introduced it as a transgene, and restored the back-to-belly pattern of mutant embryos. The same year another team put purified fly protein under rat skin; it induced cartilage, bone and marrow.

sources.citation: Um, Advances in Experimental Medicine and Biology 1077:487-499 (2018)
Urist & Strates, Journal of Dental Research 50(6):1392-1406 (1971)

image.caption: Flies have no bones, yet their BMP relative patterns their bodies and can make bone in rats.

audio.title: Corn lilies, blind cavefish and bone-making fly protein
audio.transcript:
Sonic hedgehog and bone morphogenetic protein can sound like labels invented for one textbook chapter on the spinal cord. They are not. Here are three true stories in which the wiring from this lesson turns up somewhere unexpected.

First, the high mountain meadows of Idaho in the nineteen fifties. Sheep ranchers were seeing lambs born with a single central eye. Investigators traced the problem to a tall wild plant the ewes grazed on, the corn lily, Veratrum californicum. The timing turned out to be remarkably narrow. In later dosing experiments, ewes exposed on day thirteen or fourteen of pregnancy had lambs with a range of head and face defects, including cyclopia, while lambs in the day fifteen group appeared normal. The compound clears quickly in ewes, so for cyclopia to occur the exposure has to coincide with a brief stage of development. The compound was named cyclopamine, and decades later researchers showed that it binds Smoothened directly and inhibits canonical Hedgehog signaling. That finding came to matter for people. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common human cancer, and in many of these tumors mutations disable Patched one and leave Smoothened active. Cyclopamine inspired the search that led to vismodegib, an oral Smoothened blocker approved by the F D A in twenty twelve for advanced basal cell carcinoma.

Second, a limestone cave in Mexico. Living in the dark is a pale, eyeless fish called Astyanax mexicanus. Outside, in sunlit rivers, swim silvery fish with large eyes, and they belong to the same species. In cavefish embryos, Hedgehog genes are expressed across a wider zone along the front of the midline than in river fish. The domains of Pax six, the Class One factor that Sonic hedgehog switches off in the spinal cord, are smaller and separated by a gap. That expanded Hedgehog signaling helps trigger lens cell death, so the small eyes stop growing and degenerate. When researchers boosted Sonic hedgehog in river-fish embryos during the early window when eyes are sensitive, the embryos showed abnormal eye development and more lip taste buds. Separate experiments link Sonic hedgehog to wider jaws. Wider jaws and more taste buds may help cavefish find and sample food in the dark.

Finally, if you have wondered why a protein named for bone is patterning sensory interneurons at the top of the spinal cord, blame history. In nineteen sixty-five, Marshall Urist reported that decalcified bone implanted in muscle induced new bone, and in nineteen seventy-one he and his colleague Strates called the active factor bone morphogenetic protein. Fruit flies have no bones at all, yet they use a close relative of B M P four to tell their backs from their bellies. In nineteen ninety-three, one team replaced the signaling region in a fly gene fragment with the signaling part of human B M P four, introduced it as a transgene, and restored the back-to-belly pattern of mutant embryos, evidence that this signaling machinery has been conserved for hundreds of millions of years. The same year, another team implanted purified fruit fly protein under the skin of rats, and the insect signal induced cartilage, bone and bone marrow. A boneless animal's protein built a mammal's bone. The skeleton, it seems, borrowed an older patterning signal rather than the other way round.
